passage:
Tuesday: Leela was signing up for a music app's student plan. Basic: ₹59, ads between songs. Standard: ₹169, fewer ads, one device. Premium: ₹179, no ads, four devices, offline downloads. "Ten rupees more for all that? Obviously Premium," she told Seema, and tapped.
Friday: Seema asked how many devices she used. "Just my phone." Offline downloads? "Haven't tried." Leela shrugged. "Still, it's the best value."
Next Tuesday: Her bank message showed ₹179 gone. She had meant to spend around sixty a month on music. For a second she frowned at the Standard plan, the one she would never have picked. Then she put on a song and decided she had made a smart choice.

qa.q: How many devices did Leela use?
qa.a: Just her phone.

qa.q: Why did Premium feel like the obvious choice to Leela?
qa.a: She felt confident it was clear value, because next to Standard at ₹169, Premium seemed to give everything for only ten rupees more.

qa.q: What question could Leela have asked before tapping on Tuesday?
qa.a: Which features she actually needs, since one phone and a few ads were fine, and whether she would still pay ₹179 if only Basic and Premium were shown.

qa.q: How might Seema see the Friday conversation?
qa.a: Seema's questions show Leela uses none of the extras, so to Seema the "best value" may look like paying for things Leela doesn't need. 😅

grounding: A young woman picks the premium plan because a barely cheaper middle plan makes it look like obvious value, though she uses none of its extras.

passage: Ritu, before you sign that plan, listen to an old man's story. I'm Arnab, and when I was twenty-one, a gym opened near my college hostel. The board said: one month, eight hundred rupees; three months, two thousand three hundred; one year, two thousand five hundred. Three months for 2300, or a whole year for just 200 more? I felt like a genius. I paid for the year out of my scholarship money. I went eleven times. Nobody I knew ever took the three-month plan. It just sat there looking silly, making the yearly one look like a gift. And I never even considered the monthly option, which is what I actually needed. So before you choose, cover the middle option with your thumb and see how you feel.

qa.q: How many times did Arnab go to the gym?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: Why did young Arnab feel like a genius paying for the whole year?
qa.a: The three-month plan at 2300 made the yearly one at 2500 look like a gift, so he felt sure he was getting great value.

qa.q: What does Arnab suggest Ritu try before choosing, and why?
qa.a: Covering the middle option with a thumb; without the odd plan in view, it is easier to see what is really needed, like Arnab's monthly option.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel hearing this just before signing?
qa.a: Ritu might feel a little uneasy about the plan in hand, but also grateful for a simple test to try before paying.

grounding: An older man recalls how, at twenty-one, a pointless middle gym plan made the yearly plan look like obvious value and steered his choice.

passage: Asif's final-year project files were due to his guide by midnight, and his laptop was out of storage. On the sign-up page, a red timer ticked: "Offer ends in 09:54." Plan A: 50 GB, ₹75 a month. Plan B: 100 GB, ₹210. Plan C: 2 TB, ₹220, plus photo backup and family sharing. "Karthik, ten rupees more for twenty times the space!" he said. Karthik, eating chips on the bed, said, "You need about 20 GB." The Wi-Fi dropped, then came back. The timer said 03:10. Asif chose Plan C and felt a rush of relief, as if he had beaten the system. At 11:40 p.m. he uploaded 18 GB and closed the laptop, very pleased with his bargain.

qa.q: How much space did Karthik say Asif needed?
qa.a: About 20 GB.

qa.q: What did Asif feel after choosing Plan C, and why?
qa.a: He felt relief and a sense of beating the system, because Plan B at ₹210 made Plan C at ₹220 look like a steal.

qa.q: With the timer running, what could Asif have done differently?
qa.a: He could have ignored the timer and Plan B, asked what he needed, about 20 GB, and picked Plan A, which covered his 18 GB upload.

qa.q: How does Karthik, on the bed, see the choice?
qa.a: To Karthik, the only question is how much space the project needs; away from the timer and the odd middle plan, 20 GB is the whole story.

grounding: Under deadline pressure, a student picks the top storage plan because a barely cheaper middle plan makes it look like obvious value.

passage: In a lane full of study libraries in north Delhi, Sarika, twenty, stood at the counter of a reading room with a price board. Basic: ₹800 a month, fan, shared table. Standard: ₹1,450, AC, no locker. Premium: ₹1,500, AC, locker, reserved seat, open twenty-four hours. 'Fifty rupees more for all that?' she said to Irawati. 'Premium, obviously.' She had come in wanting the basic one; she only studied mornings and lived five minutes away. But the standard plan made premium look like a gift. She paid ₹1,500 and felt sharp. A month later, Irawati asked how she liked the locker. Sarika laughed. 'I've never opened it. And I leave at one.' She had studied at night exactly zero times. That month she'd also skipped two dinners with friends because money was tight. She looked at the board again. Nobody ever picked Standard, she realised. It wasn't there to be picked.

qa.q: How much did Sarika pay for the reading room each month?
qa.a: She paid ₹1,500.

qa.q: How did Sarika feel when she looked at the board again?
qa.a: She felt a little foolish and uneasy, realising nobody ever picked Standard and that it was there only to make Premium look like a gift.

qa.q: What could Sarika have asked herself at the counter, before choosing?
qa.a: She could have asked what she actually needed, mornings only and five minutes away, and compared the plans with that instead of with the Standard plan.

qa.q: How might Irawati see Sarika's choice after a month?
qa.a: Irawati might find it funny that the locker was never opened, but also notice that paying more meant Sarika skipped dinners with friends.

grounding: A young woman picks the premium reading-room plan because a barely cheaper middle plan with much less makes premium look like obvious value, and later sees the trick.

passage:
'Aditi, which data plan should I take? My phone plan ends tonight.'
'Show me, Zainab.'
'Plan one, one-ninety-nine, one GB a day. Plan two, four-forty-nine, one and a half GB. Plan three, four-seventy-nine, three GB a day plus a free video plan.'
'You use one GB a day, max.'
'But look at plan two! Thirty rupees less than plan three and half the data. Who takes plan two?'
'Nobody. That's the point.'
'What point?'
'Why would they make a plan nobody takes?'
'So I take plan three, obviously.'
'Or so you forget plan one exists.'
Zainab paused, thumb over the button. 'Plan one doesn't have the video thing.'
'Do you watch videos on your phone?'
'...Sometimes.'
'You watch on Abbu's TV.'
'Four-seventy-nine is still better value.'
Her big sister Aditi sighed. Zainab pressed plan three and felt clever for the whole evening.

qa.q: How much was plan three?
qa.a: Plan three was four-seventy-nine, with three GB a day plus a free video plan.

qa.q: Why was Zainab so sure plan three was 'obviously' right?
qa.a: Compared with plan two, which was only thirty rupees less for half the data, plan three looked like clear value, so she felt confident and clever.

qa.q: At which moment could Zainab have made a better choice, and how?
qa.a: When Aditi said she uses one GB a day at most, Zainab could have compared plan three with plan one and her real needs instead of with plan two.

qa.q: How does Aditi see the plan nobody takes?
qa.a: Aditi sees plan two as a trick to make plan three look good and to make people forget the cheaper plan that fits them.

grounding: At home a young woman picks the priciest data plan because a barely cheaper middle plan with much less makes it look like obvious value, despite her sister's hints.
